question: The 37% Rule
content: The 37% Rule states that in optimal stopping problems, you should look at and reject the first 37% of options, then choose the next option that is better than all previously seen options.
description: You are apartment hunting in a competitive market with 30 days to find a place. According to the 37% Rule, what should you do?
options: Look at apartments for the first 11 days without committing, then rent the first place that is better than any you've seen so far
Rent the first apartment you see to avoid missing out on the opportunity entirely because waiting any longer makes no sense in this market
Look at all thirty available apartments before making your final decision
Rent the fifteenth apartment you see regardless of its quality or price
answer: Look at apartments for the first 11 days without committing, then rent the first place that is better than any you've seen so far
explanation: 37% of 30 days is approximately 11 days. During this look phase, you gather data about what constitutes a good apartment. After day 11, you commit to the first apartment that surpasses all previous options.

question: Look-Then-Leap Rule
content: The Look-Then-Leap Rule involves two phases: first looking (gathering data without committing) and then leaping (committing to the first option that exceeds the best seen during the look phase).
description: You are dating and want to maximize your chances of finding the best partner. You plan to date seriously for 2 years before settling down. How should you apply the Look-Then-Leap Rule?
options: Date casually for 2 years, then marry the next person who is better than anyone you've dated so far
Marry the first person you date to avoid the loneliness of being single and the uncertainty of continued searching
Spend exactly two years dating everyone before making a selection
Marry after dating ten people regardless of their overall quality
answer: Date casually for 2 years, then marry the next person who is better than anyone you've dated so far
explanation: With a 2-year look phase, you date without committing to establish what makes a good partner. After 2 years, you leap by committing to the first person who exceeds all previous partners in your estimation.

question: Optimal Stopping Under Variable Sample Sizes
content: The 37% Rule assumes a known number of total options N, with equal value in each observation. In real-world scenarios, N is often uncertain and each observation has a cost.
description: A product manager is A/B testing which of many possible features to ship. Each feature test costs $10,000 and takes 2 weeks. The expected value of the best feature is $500,000. She can test up to 50 features but doesn't know if there are actually 50 viable candidates. How should the cost of testing and uncertainty about N modify the classical 37% Rule?
options: The look phase should be shorter than 37% because each observation has a significant cost and the search should terminate when the expected improvement from continued searching falls below the cost of the next test

The standard 37% rule still applies exactly regardless of testing costs and variable sample sizes because the mathematical ratio 1/e remains universally optimal regardless of the cost of each observation or the uncertainty about how many total options exist
The look phase should be extended beyond 37% to compensate for the uncertainty about how many options actually exist
The product manager should test all fifty available features to completely eliminate uncertainty about the number of options
answer: The look phase should be shorter than 37% because each observation has a significant cost and the search should terminate when the expected improvement from continued searching falls below the cost of the next test
explanation: When observations have costs, you cannot afford to observe a fixed fraction of options for free. The optimal strategy requires a dynamic threshold: stop searching when the marginal expected benefit of one more observation is less than its cost ($10,000). This effectively creates an early-stopping condition that typically results in a shorter look phase, especially if early options are reasonably good.

question: Full Information vs. No Information
content: In full information optimal stopping, you know the absolute quality of options; in no information, you only know relative rankings compared to what you've seen.
description: When selling your house, you can compare offers to recent sales data (full information). What strategy should you use?
options: Set a minimum acceptable price threshold and accept the first offer that meets it
Wait for the highest possible offer regardless of how long it might take or whether one ever comes
Accept the very first offer you receive without comparing to other options
Flip a coin to decide whether to accept or reject each offer
answer: Set a minimum acceptable price threshold and accept the first offer that meets it
explanation: With full information (knowing market values), you should use a threshold strategy: set your minimum acceptable price based on comparable sales and accept the first offer that meets or exceeds it.

question: Finite Horizons
content: Finite horizon optimal stopping problems have a known endpoint, which affects the optimal strategy compared to infinite horizon problems.
description: You need to hire a contractor for a 3-month project starting in June. How should the finite horizon affect your hiring strategy?
options: Be more selective early and less selective as the deadline approaches
Be less selective early and more selective as the deadline approaches
Interview exactly three contractors and pick the best among them
Hire the first contractor who is available to start immediately
answer: Be more selective early and less selective as the deadline approaches
explanation: With a finite horizon (knowing you must hire by a certain date), you should be more selective early in the search and become less selective as the deadline approaches to avoid being left without options.

question: No-Recall Constraints
content: No-recall constraints mean that once you reject an option, you cannot return to it later, which is realistic for many real-world decisions like dating or apartment hunting.
description: You are shopping at a flea market and see a unique vintage jacket. Why might you buy it immediately despite wanting to keep looking?
options: Because if you pass on it, you cannot return to buy it later (no-recall constraint)
Because it is definitely the best jacket available at the flea market and you should trust your instincts
Because flea market items never go on sale at any point in time
Because you have unlimited time to decide what to purchase later
answer: Because if you pass on it, you cannot return to buy it later (no-recall constraint)
explanation: In no-recall scenarios like flea markets, once an item is purchased by someone else, it is gone forever. This creates pressure to act when you see something uniquely valuable.

question: End-of-Life Buffers
content: End-of-life buffers involve adjusting decisions based on remaining time or opportunities, such as being more willing to try new things when young versus sticking with favorites when older.
description: A 70-year-old is choosing between trying a risky new medication with potential cure versus sticking with current treatment. How should remaining life expectancy affect this decision?
options: They should be more willing to try the new treatment because they have less to lose
They should stick with current treatment because they have less time to recover from risks
Age should not affect medical decisions in any meaningful way
They should flip a coin to decide which treatment option to pursue
answer: They should stick with current treatment because they have less time to recover from risks
explanation: With limited remaining life, the potential downside of a risky new treatment (time spent recovering from side effects) represents a larger proportion of remaining life, making established treatments relatively more attractive.

question: "The Typist's Dilemma"
content: The Typists Dilemma applies optimal stopping to editing: knowing when to stop improving a document and declare it finished, balancing perfectionism against completion.
description: You are writing a report and notice minor typos. According to optimal stopping principles, when should you stop editing?
options: When the time spent correcting errors exceeds the expected improvement in quality
When you have corrected every single typo and grammatical mistake in the document
When you have spent exactly two hours editing the document
Never stop editing until the document is completely perfect
answer: When the time spent correcting errors exceeds the expected improvement in quality
explanation: Optimal stopping for editing means continuing to improve the document only as long as the expected benefit exceeds the cost. When additional editing yields diminishing returns, it is time to leap and declare the work finished.
